name: Didactic Definition Profiling
description: Identifies the unnecessary, formulaic insertion of definitions. AI models compulsively define terms (e.g., 'X is defined as Y') to maximize clarity and helpfulness, whereas humans assume shared background knowledge.
algorithm: Syntactic Definition Extraction & Pragmatic Necessity Scoring
mechanism: Modern Large Language Models, particularly those refined via Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), are heavily penalized for being vague and rewarded for being 'helpful' and educational. This creates a deeply ingrained pathological behavior: the 'didactic tic'. When generating text, AI models frequently interrupt the narrative flow to explicitly define terms, concepts, or acronyms, even when writing for an expert audience. They rely on highly formulaic syntactical structures such as 'X is a...', 'In the context of Y, X refers to...', or appositives like 'X, which is...'. Humans, conversely, rely heavily on 'common ground'—the implicit shared knowledge between writer and reader. A human writing a professional email about 'SEO' will simply use the term; an AI is statistically likely to expand it to 'Search Engine Optimization (SEO), the process of...'. This NLP method scans for these explicit definition clauses and calculates their frequency relative to the assumed expertise level of the text. An abnormally high density of unsolicited definitions strongly flags the text as machine-generated.
useCase: Analyzing professional emails, opinion pieces, and creative writing where the sudden, textbook-style definition of common terms disrupts the natural conversational flow and betrays an AI's 'helpfulness' bias.
strengths:
• Highly accurate at detecting the 'helpful assistant' persona fundamentally baked into major commercial LLMs (ChatGPT, Claude).
• Extremely robust against simple paraphrasing, because the underlying psychological urge of the model to 'explain' remains intact.
• Serves as an excellent heuristic for identifying AI-generated filler content ('fluff') used to meet word counts.
limitations:
• Susceptible to false positives in genuinely educational human writing, such as textbooks, introductory tutorials, or glossaries.
• Effectiveness drops if the AI is explicitly prompted with strict constraints like 'Do not explain basic concepts' or 'Write for a postdoctoral audience'.
• Relies on syntactic parsing; highly conversational or slang-based definitions might evade the structural detector.
parameters:
Analysis: Syntactic Clause Parsing (Appositives, Copular Verbs) & Entity Mapping
Metric: Solicitous Definition Ratio per 1,000 Words
Output: 0-100 Didactic Over-Explanation (Helpfulness Bias) Score
accuracy: High — 75-85%. One of the most reliable semantic signatures of RLHF-aligned models, acting as a dead giveaway of synthetic authorship in casual or expert-level contexts.

references.title: Guo, B. et al. (2023). How Close is ChatGPT to Human Experts? Comparison Corpus, Evaluation, and Detection. NeurIPS.
Bai, Y. et al. (2022). Training a Helpful and Harmless Assistant with Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback. arXiv.
